claim: TurboID and miniTurbo are highly active biotin ligase variants that enable proximity labeling in plants.
source: Recent technological improvements, namely two highly active biotin ligase variants (TurboID and miniTurbo), allowed us to address two challenging questions in plants
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing biotinylation activity in N. benthamiana and Arabidopsis

claim: TurboID can identify in vivo partners of a low abundant key developmental transcription factor (FAMA).
source: what are in vivo partners of a low abundant key developmental transcription factor
evidence: Demonstrated through FAMA-TurboID proximity labeling experiments identifying known and novel interactors

claim: Proteins identified with FAMA-TurboID include known interactors of this stomatal transcription factor and novel proteins that could facilitate its activator and repressor functions.
source: Proteins identified with FAMA-TurboID include known interactors of this stomatal transcription factor and novel proteins that could facilitate its activator and repressor functions.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data identifying 47 high-confidence candidates including transcriptional regulators and co-repressors

claim: TurboID enables purification of cell type- and subcellular compartment-specific proteins when directed to stomatal nuclei.
source: Directing TurboID to stomatal nuclei enabled purification of cell type- and subcellular compartment-specific proteins.
evidence: Demonstrated by identifying 394 proteins enriched in FAMA-expressing cell nuclei

claim: TurboID and miniTurbo work in Arabidopsis and Nicotiana benthamiana.
source: Broad tests of TurboID and miniTurbo in Arabidopsis and Nicotiana benthamiana
evidence: Demonstrated through immunoblot analysis showing protein biotinylation in both species

claim: BioID-based proximity labeling has been limited primarily to systems employing transient and/or high expression in plants.
source: Although the potential utility for PL in plants is equally tremendous, its adaptation in plants has been slower, with the successes being limited primarily to systems employing transient and/or high expression.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous plant BioID studies

claim: The first three plant proximity labeling studies utilized BioID based on E. coli biotin ligase BirA with R118G mutation.
source: The first three of these (Lin et al., 2017; Khan et al., 2018; Conlan et al., 2018) utilized BioID, which is based on an Escherichia coli biotin ligase (BirA) made promiscuous by a point mutation (R118G) to yield BirA*.
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: The labeling radius of BirA* is approximately 10 nm based on nuclear pore complex experiments.
source: Based on experiments with the nuclear pore complex (Kim et al., 2014), the labeling radius of BirA* was estimated to be approximately 10 nm, which is in the size-range of an average globular protein.
evidence: Based on cited experimental work in mammalian cells

claim: Cell walls, cuticle, growth temperature optima, and endogenous biotin production provide major impediments to BioID-based proximity labeling in plants.
source: Structural features of plants, including cell walls and the cuticle, most plants' growth temperature optima and the fact that plants produce and store biotin in their cells, provide major impediments to BioID-based PL systems (Bontinck et al., 2018).
evidence: Based on cited review and general plant biology knowledge

claim: TurboID was successfully used in tobacco plants while this work was in review.
source: While this work was in review, a new manuscript demonstrating the effectiveness of TurboID in tobacco plants (Zhang et al., 2019) was published.
evidence: Citation to concurrent published work

claim: The potential of TurboID to identify rare protein complexes or local proteomes in individual cell types of a complex multicellular organism had not yet been addressed prior to this work.
source: Moreover, the potential of TurboID to identify rare protein complexes or local proteomes in individual cell types of a complex multicellular organisms had not yet been addressed.
evidence: Statement about gap in literature at time of submission

claim: TurboID and miniTurbo induce strong labeling of proteins in N. benthamiana and Arabidopsis after biotin treatment.
source: In TbID- and mTb-expressing N. benthamiana and Arabidopsis, biotin treatment induced strong labeling of proteins, demonstrating that the new biotin ligases work under our chosen conditions in plants.
evidence: Demonstrated by streptavidin immunoblots shown in Figure 1B-C

claim: TurboID and miniTurbo show greatly increased activity compared to BirA* in plants.
source: As was observed in other organisms, both TbID and mTb showed greatly increased activity compared to BirA*, which mainly achieved weak self-labeling within 1 h of biotin treatment (Figure 1B–C, Figure 1—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: Shown by immunoblot comparison in figures

claim: Background labeling from endogenous biotin is negligible in most cases for TurboID and miniTurbo in plants.
source: Since plants produce and store free biotin in their cells, we were concerned about 'background' labeling in the absence of exogenous biotin. Although it did appear, background labeling was in most cases negligible.
evidence: Observed in immunoblot experiments comparing treated and untreated samples

claim: TurboID is more active than miniTurbo but produces more background in Arabidopsis.
source: In Arabidopsis, however, TbID was clearly more active than mTb but also produced more background.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoblot comparison in Figure 1C and supplements

claim: Enhanced activity of TurboID in the absence of exogenous biotin is especially evident in lines with low expression levels.
source: Enhanced activity of TbID in the absence of exogenous biotin was especially evident in lines that express TbID and mTb at low levels (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Shown in immunoblots comparing strong and weak expression lines

claim: No significant differences in labeling efficiency were observed between nuclear and cytosolic TurboID/miniTurbo constructs at the resolution of immunoblots.
source: Comparing nuclear and cytosolic constructs, we did not observe any significant differences in labeling efficiency at the resolution of immunoblots (Figure 1—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: Based on immunoblot analysis of different subcellular localizations

claim: TurboID induces labeling of proteins over background levels within 15-30 minutes of treatment with biotin at room temperature in Arabidopsis.
source: TbID induced labeling of proteins over background levels within 15–30 min of treatment with 250 or 50 µM biotin at room temperature (22°C) and labeling steadily increased over the next 3 to 5 h (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by time course immunoblot experiments

claim: TurboID self-labeling is evident after as little as 5 minutes of biotin treatment.
source: An increase in self-labeling of TbID was evident even earlier, after as little as 5 min (compare Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Shown in immunoblot time course

claim: miniTurbo shows clear labeling of proteins within 10 minutes of treatment with 50 µM biotin in N. benthamiana.
source: Time course experiments in N. benthamiana suggest that mTb is equally fast, with clear labeling of proteins visible within 10 min of treatment with 50 µM biotin (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoblot time course in tobacco

claim: TurboID and miniTurbo labeling is much faster than BirA*, which required 24 hour labeling times in previous plant experiments.
source: This is a significant improvement over BirA*, for which labeling times of 24 h were applied in all three published plant experiments (Khan et al., 2018; Conlan et al., 2018; Lin et al., 2017).
evidence: Comparison to cited previous studies

claim: The activity of TurboID and miniTurbo is nearly as high at 22°C as at 30°C in Arabidopsis.
source: Encouragingly, the activity of both variants was nearly as high at 22°C as at 30°C.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoblot comparison at different temperatures in Figure 2B

claim: TurboID shows only a moderate increase of activity at 37°C compared to lower temperatures.
source: Moreover, TbID showed only a moderate increase of activity at 37°C, while mTb activity was actually reduced at this temperature (Figure 2B).
evidence: Shown in temperature comparison immunoblots

claim: miniTurbo activity is reduced at 37°C compared to 22-30°C.
source: Moreover, TbID showed only a moderate increase of activity at 37°C, while mTb activity was actually reduced at this temperature (Figure 2B).
evidence: Shown in temperature comparison immunoblots

claim: Increasing temperatures above plant growth conditions is not needed to improve TurboID/miniTurbo labeling.
source: Increasing temperatures above plant growth conditions to improve labeling is therefore not needed.
evidence: Inferred from temperature dependency experiments showing good activity at ambient temperatures

claim: Endogenous levels of biotin in plants are sufficient for low-level labeling of proteins by TurboID.
source: Endogenous levels of biotin in plants are sufficient for low-level labeling of proteins by TbID, and to some extent also by mTb.
evidence: Observed in untreated control samples showing background labeling

claim: TurboID has a larger dynamic range than miniTurbo in response to biotin concentration.
source: We found that TbID has a larger dynamic range than mTb.
evidence: Demonstrated by biotin titration experiments in Figure 2C

claim: TurboID shows weak over-background labeling with 0.5 µM biotin and is saturated at 50-75 µM biotin.
source: Weak over-background labeling could already be seen with 0.5 µM biotin, which increased weakly through 20 µM, followed by a steeper increase with 30 µM and was more or less saturated at 50–75 µM.
evidence: Shown in biotin concentration titration immunoblots

claim: miniTurbo requires between 2.5 and 10 µM biotin for weak activity and is saturated at 50-75 µM.
source: mTb required between 2.5 and 10 µM biotin for weak activity, showed a steep increase with 20 µM (comparable to TbID) and was also saturated at 50–75 µM (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Demonstrated by biotin titration experiments

claim: Vacuum infiltration is not necessary for biotin uptake in Arabidopsis seedlings.
source: At least in Arabidopsis seedlings, this is not necessary. Simply submerging the plantlets in the biotin solution resulted in the same amount of labeling as vacuum infiltration followed by incubation in the biotin solution did (Figure 2D).
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing infiltrated and non-infiltrated samples in immunoblots

claim: TurboID works well in 4- to 14-day-old plate-grown Arabidopsis seedlings without significant increase of background over time.
source: Labeling worked well in 4- to 14-day-old plate-grown seedlings without significant increase of background (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Shown in immunoblots of seedlings at different developmental stages

claim: TurboID works in separated roots and shoots of 6- to 14-day-old Arabidopsis seedlings.
source: The same was true for separated roots and shoots of 6- to 14-day-old seedlings
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoblots of separated tissue types

claim: TurboID works in rosette leaves and flower buds of adult Arabidopsis plants grown on soil.
source: and even for rosette leaves and flower buds of adult Arabidopsis plants grown on soil (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3)
evidence: Shown in immunoblots of mature plant tissues

claim: Vacuum infiltration improves TurboID labeling in unopened floral buds compared to submergence alone.
source: Vacuum infiltration was not required for the tested plant sample types, except for unopened floral buds, where infiltration improved labeling relative to submergence in the biotin solution (Figure 3).
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing infiltrated and non-infiltrated flower buds in immunoblots

claim: FAMA is a nuclear basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor expressed in young stomatal guard cells.
source: FAMA is a nuclear basic helix-loop-helix (bHLH) transcription factor (TF) that is expressed in young stomatal guard cells (GCs) in the epidermis of developing aerial tissues (Ohashi-Ito and Bergmann, 2006).
evidence: Based on cited previous characterization of FAMA

claim: The low abundance of FAMA and FAMA-expressing cells makes identification of interaction partners challenging by traditional methods.
source: The low abundance of FAMA and FAMA-expressing cells renders identification of interaction partners and cell-type-specific nuclear proteins by traditional methods challenging
evidence: Inferred from general limitations of traditional methods for rare proteins

claim: Potential FAMA interaction partners were previously identified in yeast-2-hybrid and bimolecular fluorescence complementation studies.
source: Potential FAMA interaction partners were previously identified in yeast-2-hybrid (Y2H) and bimolecular fluorescence complementation studies (Chen et al., 2016; Kanaoka et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2014; Li et al., 2018; Matos et al., 2014; Ohashi-Ito and Bergmann, 2006), but only few have been confirmed by in vivo functional data.
evidence: Based on citations to previous interaction studies

claim: The FAMA-TurboID-Venus construct is functional and complements the seedling-lethal phenotype of the fama-1 mutant.
source: The FAMA-TbID-Venus construct is functional, since it complements the seedling-lethal phenotype of the fama-1 mutant (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by rescue of mutant phenotype shown in figure supplement

claim: FAMA auto-labeling by FAMA-TurboID is observed after as little as 5 minutes of biotin treatment.
source: FAMA auto-labeling could be observed after as little as 5 min but clear labeling of other proteins required approximately 15 to 30 min.
evidence: Observed in time course immunoblot experiments

claim: Longer biotin incubation with FAMA-TurboID leads to further increase in labeling up to 3 hours.
source: Longer incubation led to further increase in labeling up to 3 h, both in the form of stronger discrete bands and of diffuse labeling, but stayed more or less the same thereafter (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Shown in time course immunoblots

claim: Proximity labeling with FAMA-TurboID identified 47 high-confidence candidate interactors after filtering.
source: This left us with 47 'high confidence' candidates (Figure 5, Table 1)
evidence: Result of mass spectrometry analysis and statistical filtering

claim: 35 of the 47 FAMA-TurboID candidates were previously demonstrated to be nuclear or found in nuclear proteome studies.
source: 35 of which were previously demonstrated to be in the nucleus using fluorescent protein fusions or were found in MS-based nuclear proteome studies (Figure 5, Table 1, Supplementary file 2 – Tables 2 and 4).
evidence: Based on literature curation and database searches

claim: More than half of the FAMA candidate proteins have a role in regulation of transcription or are chaperones.
source: Notably, more than half of the candidates have a role in regulation of transcription or are chaperones which could assist in FAMA's role as a TF or in protein folding and stabilization, respectively (Figure 5, Table 1, Supplementary file 2 – Table 4).
evidence: Based on functional annotation of identified proteins

claim: Proximity labeling identified ICE1 as a FAMA interactor, confirming previous findings.
source: Among the TFs we again found ICE1 (as well as peptides shared between ICE1 and its orthologue SCRM2).
evidence: ICE1 is a known FAMA heterodimerization partner identified by mass spectrometry

claim: Proximity labeling identified three bHLH transcription factors (AIB/JAM1, JAM3, and BIM1) as FAMA candidates.
source: We also found three other bHLH TFs (AIB/JAM1, JAM3, and BIM1)
evidence: Identified through mass spectrometry analysis of FAMA-TurboID samples

claim: BZR1, a non-canonical bHLH-type transcription factor, was identified as a FAMA candidate.
source: and the non-canonical bHLH-type TF BZR1
evidence: Identified through mass spectrometry analysis

claim: AIB and JAM3 play partially redundant roles in negative regulation of jasmonic acid signaling.
source: AIB and JAM3 play partially redundant roles in negative regulation of jasmonic acid (JA) signaling (Sasaki-Sekimoto et al., 2013; Fonseca et al., 2014)
evidence: Based on cited publications

claim: BIM1 and BZR1 mediate brassinosteroid signaling.
source: while BIM1 and BZR1 mediate brassinosteroid (BR) signaling (Yin et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2002)
evidence: Based on cited publications

claim: Both jasmonic acid and brassinosteroid signaling play roles in stomatal function or development.
source: Both JA and BR signaling play roles in stomatal function or development (Acharya and Assmann, 2009; Gudesblat et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2012).
evidence: Based on cited publications

claim: MED16, a component of the mediator complex, was identified as a FAMA candidate transcriptional co-activator.
source: Among the transcriptional co-regulators we found two significantly enriched transcriptional co-activators: MED16, which is part of the mediator complex that links TFs to RNA Pol II (Kidd et al., 2011)
evidence: Identified by mass spectrometry and annotated based on literature

claim: HAC1, a histone acetyl transferase, was identified as a FAMA candidate transcriptional co-activator.
source: and HAC1, which is a histone acetyl transferase (HAT) (Deng et al., 2007)
evidence: Identified by mass spectrometry and annotated based on literature

claim: FAMA activates genes both directly by recruiting RNA Pol II and by opening up chromatin for other transcriptional regulators.
source: Combined with previous data showing a link between FAMA and RNA Pol II (Chen et al., 2016), this suggests that FAMA activates genes both directly by recruiting RNA Pol II and by opening up the chromatin for other transcriptional regulators.
evidence: Inferred from identification of MED16 and HAC1 combined with previous data

claim: TPR3 and TPR4, TOPLESS-related transcriptional co-repressors, were identified as FAMA candidates.
source: Among transcriptional co-repressors were TOPLESS (TPL)-related proteins TPR3 and TPR4
evidence: Identified by mass spectrometry

claim: LEUNIG (LUG) and LEUNIG HOMOLOG (LUH), which recruit histone deacetylases to transcription factors, were identified as FAMA candidates.
source: and LEUNIG (LUG) and LEUNIG HOMOLOG (LUH), which recruit histone deacetylases (HDACs) to TFs (Long et al., 2006)
evidence: Identified by mass spectrometry and annotated based on literature

claim: SEUSS (SEU), a linker protein that mediates interaction of LUG and LUH with transcription factors, was identified as a FAMA candidate.
source: Additionally, we identified the linker protein SEUSS (SEU), which mediates interaction of LUG and LUH with TFs (Liu and Karmarkar, 2008; Sitaraman et al., 2008).
evidence: Identified by mass spectrometry and annotated based on literature

claim: The identification of all three members of the SEU/LUG/LUH co-repressor complex is a strong indication of a functional complex with FAMA in the plant.
source: The identification of all three members of the SEU/LUG/LUH co-repressor complex is a strong indication of a functional complex with FAMA in the plant.
evidence: Inferred from identification of all three complex components together

claim: BIM1 and SEU are direct interaction partners of FAMA based on yeast-2-hybrid and proximity labeling validation experiments.
source: Our experiments suggest that BIM1 and SEU are direct interaction partners of FAMA
evidence: Demonstrated by Y2H and pairwise PL assays shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5

claim: LUH and BZR1 might be in indirect contact with FAMA or require a specific protein or DNA context for interaction.
source: while LUH and BZR1 might be in indirect contact with FAMA or require a specific protein or DNA context to be present for interaction.
evidence: Inferred from weak or absent interaction in validation experiments

claim: Proximity labeling is superior to affinity purification-mass spectrometry for identification of FAMA interactors.
source: our 'FAMA interactome' experiment demonstrates the usefulness of PL to identify potential interaction partners of rare proteins
evidence: Comparison of PL results to AP-MS results showing PL identified more candidates

claim: Most FAMA interaction candidates were identified at the 3 hour time point.
source: It is worth noting, that most FAMA interaction candidates were identified at the 3 h time point
evidence: Observed in the distribution of candidates across time points

claim: Longer biotin treatment greatly improved identification of biotinylated proteins in the FAMA experiment.
source: and that longer biotin treatment greatly improved identification of biotinylated proteins (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 4, Supplementary file 2 – Table 3).
evidence: Shown by comparing number of identified proteins at different time points

claim: 394 proteins were significantly enriched in FAMAnucTbID compared to wild-type.
source: Despite the relative rareness of FAMA-expressing cells, the FAMAnucTbID dataset yielded 394 proteins that were enriched compared to WT (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 3, Supplementary file 3 – Table 3).
evidence: Result of mass spectrometry analysis and statistical testing

claim: 2,215 proteins were significantly enriched in UBQnucTbID compared to wild-type, comprising the global nuclear protein dataset.
source: 2215 proteins were significantly enriched in UBQnucTbID compared to WT (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 3, Supplementary file 3 – Table 2). These proteins comprise our 'global' nuclear protein dataset.
evidence: Result of mass spectrometry analysis and statistical testing

claim: Most proteins enriched in FAMAnucTbID overlap with the global nuclear protein dataset.
source: Notably, most of them overlap with our global nuclear protein dataset (Figure 6), as would be expected since the UBQnucTbID dataset also contains FAMA-stage cells.
evidence: Shown in Venn diagram and inferred from experimental design

claim: More than three quarters of proteins enriched in UBQnucTbID and FAMAnucTbID datasets are experimentally verified nuclear proteins or predicted to be nuclear.
source: More than three quarters of the proteins enriched in our UBQnucTbID and FAMAnucTbID datasets are either experimentally verified nuclear proteins or are predicted to be localized in the nucleus (Supplementary file 3 – Tables 2, 3 and 5).
evidence: Based on comparison to curated nuclear protein databases and prediction tools

claim: Chloroplast proteins make up only about 4% of identified nuclear proteins based on experimental and prediction data.
source: Chloroplast proteins, which are a major source of contamination in plant MS experiments, make up only about 4% of our identified proteins based on experimental and prediction data (Supplementary file 3 – Table 5).
evidence: Based on subcellular localization annotation of identified proteins

claim: Nuclear TurboID successfully labeled all major sub-nuclear compartments and domains including nuclear pore complex, nuclear envelope, nuclear lamina, nucleolus and chromatin-associated proteins.
source: Importantly, our nuclear TbID successfully labeled all major sub-nuclear compartments and domains, including the nuclear pore complex, the nuclear envelope, the nuclear lamina, the nucleolus and other small speckles, as well as DNA- and chromatin-associated proteins (subdomain markers from Petrovská et al., 2015; Tamura and Hara-Nishimura, 2013, see Supplementary file 3 – Table 8 for examples).
evidence: Based on identification of known markers for different nuclear subdomains

claim: Known stomatal lineage and guard cell-associated transcription factors FAMA, HDG2, and SCAP1 were found among FAMA-nuclei enriched proteins.
source: Indeed, looking at proteins that were equally abundant or slightly enriched in the FAMAnucTbID samples, we find several known stomatal lineage- and GC-associated TFs, namely FAMA itself, HOMEODOMAIN GLABROUS 2 (HDG2) and STOMATAL CARPENTER 1 (SCAP1) (Ohashi-Ito and Bergmann, 2006; Peterson et al., 2013; Negi et al., 2013).
evidence: Identified in mass spectrometry data and annotated based on literature

claim: 10 of the 44 highly FAMAnucTbID enriched proteins were previously identified in the guard cell proteome by Zhao and colleagues.
source: Additionally, there were 10 proteins among the 44 highly FAMAnucTbID enriched proteins, that were previously identified as part of the GC proteome by Zhao and colleagues using MS analysis of 300 million GC protoplasts (Zhao et al., 2010; Zhao et al., 2008) (Supplementary file 3 – Tables 3 and 6).
evidence: Based on comparison to published guard cell proteome

claim: Neither FAMA nor SCAP1 are in the Zhao guard cell protoplast proteome, presumably due to their relatively low expression.
source: It is worth noting that neither FAMA nor SCAP1 are in the Zhao GC protoplast proteome, presumably due to their relatively low expression and the use of material from more mature plants.
evidence: Inferred from comparison to published proteome and knowledge of protein expression

claim: Proximity labeling can find lowly expressed proteins that are missed by traditional proteomics approaches.
source: These results suggest that PL can find lowly expressed proteins
evidence: Inferred from identification of FAMA and SCAP1 which were not in previous GC proteome

claim: Free biotin in protein extracts competes with biotinylated proteins for binding to streptavidin beads.
source: The inclusion of a biotin-depletion step was found to be critical as free biotin in the protein extracts competes with biotinylated proteins for binding of the streptavidin beads (Figure 4—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing pulldown efficiency with and without biotin depletion

claim: Thorough washing of cells is not sufficient to remove free biotin from intact plant tissue.
source: While for mammalian cell culture or rice protoplasts thorough washing of the cells seems to suffice for removal of free biotin, this is not the case for intact plant tissue (see also Conlan et al., 2018; Khan et al., 2018).
evidence: Based on experimental observations and cited previous plant studies

claim: On-beads tryptic digest yields significantly higher protein amounts and more protein identifications than elution followed by in-gel digestion.
source: Tryptic digest for LC-MS/MS analysis was done on-beads, since test experiments revealed that elution from the beads using two different methods (Cheah and Yamada, 2017; Schopp and Béthune, 2018) and subsequent in-gel digestion of biotinylated proteins yielded significantly lower protein amounts and less protein identifications (data not shown).
evidence: Based on comparison of different sample preparation methods

claim: Highly biotinylated proteins interact with more than one streptavidin molecule and are especially hard to elute from beads.
source: Notably, highly biotinylated proteins, which likely comprise the most interesting candidates, will interact with more than one streptavidin molecule and will be especially hard to elute.
evidence: Inferred from understanding of biotin-streptavidin interaction and experimental observations

claim: Affinity purification-mass spectrometry with FAMA-CFP failed to identify transcriptional regulators beyond ICE1 despite use of crosslinking and large amounts of plant material.
source: Apart from INDUCER OF CBF EXPRESSION 1 (ICE1), which is a known heterodimerization partner of FAMA (Kanaoka et al., 2008), we failed to identify any transcriptional (co-)regulators by AP-MS with FAMA-CFP, despite the use of crosslinking agents and large amounts of plant material (15 g of 4-day-old seedlings per sample).
evidence: Result of AP-MS experiments performed as control

claim: Less than 20% of FAMA AP-MS candidates were predicted to be nuclear.
source: Moreover, less than 20% of the AP-MS-derived 'candidates' were predicted to be nuclear, and one quarter were chloroplast proteins (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 2 – Table 5).
evidence: Based on subcellular localization prediction of AP-MS identified proteins

claim: One quarter of FAMA AP-MS candidates were chloroplast proteins.
source: Moreover, less than 20% of the AP-MS-derived 'candidates' were predicted to be nuclear, and one quarter were chloroplast proteins (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 2 – Table 5).
evidence: Based on subcellular localization prediction of AP-MS identified proteins

claim: A large proportion of proteins identified by proximity labeling bound to beads non-specifically.
source: Despite this clear separation, the majority of proteins were common to all samples, including the untreated WT control (Supplementary file 2 – Table 1), and moreover, were unchanged between samples (Figure 5—figure supplements 2 and 3). This indicates that a large proportion of identified proteins bound to the beads non-specifically.
evidence: Inferred from proteins being present in all samples including controls

claim: Non-specific binding of proteins to beads is not uncommon for affinity purification experiments.
source: This is not uncommon for affinity purification experiments, and underlines the importance of appropriate controls and data filtering pipelines.
evidence: Based on general knowledge of affinity purification methods

claim: RBR1, a cell cycle regulator and known FAMA interactor, was enriched in FAMA-TurboID samples but did not pass stringent filtering criteria.
source: RBR1, a cell cycle regulator and a known interactor of FAMA (Lee et al., 2014; Matos et al., 2014), is also among the FAMA-TbID enriched proteins but, due to a modest fold change, did not pass our last filters (Figure 5, – Supplementary file 2 Table 2).
evidence: Observed in mass spectrometry data with modest enrichment

claim: Stringent filtering cutoffs may cause loss of some true interactors, especially ubiquitously expressed proteins with many partners.
source: This suggests that by setting a stringent cutoff on enrichment between FAMA-TbID and FAMAnucTbID, we might lose some true interactors. This might be especially true of ubiquitously expressed proteins with many partners like RBR1, where FAMA-RBR1 interactions are likely to represent only a small fraction of all complexes.
evidence: Inferred from RBR1 example and understanding of protein interaction networks

claim: TurboID is suitable for studying subcellular proteomes on a whole-plant as well as cell-type-specific level.
source: Overall, this experiment demonstrates the usefulness of TbID as a tool for studying subcellular proteomes on a whole-plant as well as on a cell-type-specific level.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from successful nuclear proteome experiments

claim: TurboID and miniTurbo enable effective proximity labeling in a wide variety of tissues and expression levels in plants.
source: Here, we show that TurboID and miniTurbo enable effective PL in a wide variety of tissues and expression levels in plants.
evidence: Demonstrated through experiments in different tissues and developmental stages

claim: The work provides reagents and a broadly applicable workflow for proximity labeling experiments in Arabidopsis and Nicotiana benthamiana.
source: To enable adoption by the plant research community, we provide reagents and a broadly applicable workflow for PL experiments under different experimental conditions in a variety of tissues in Arabidopsis and Nicotiana benthamiana and highlight critical steps in experimental design and execution.
evidence: Description of provided tools and protocols
